_about: The Write page's format guide (docs/SCREENPLAY-WRITER-PLAN.md, Phase 3). Content, not code: src/lib/format-rules.js reads the lists and the copy from here, so a sentence can be reworded without touching a check. A rule's `id` is what a dismissed note is remembered by for the session; renaming one only un-dismisses it. `severity` is `warn` (a reader will trip on it) or `hint` (a convention worth knowing). `why` is written for somebody writing their first screenplay.

rules.message: Start the scene heading with INT. or EXT.
rules.why: INT. (inside) or EXT. (outside) is the first thing a heading tells the crew: whether this scene needs a roof, a permit or the weather. Use INT./EXT. for a car or a doorway, and EST. for an establishing shot.

rules.message: End the heading with the time of day — DAY, NIGHT, CONTINUOUS…
rules.why: The time closes the heading after a dash: INT. KITCHEN – NIGHT. The assistant director schedules the shoot from it, and a reader uses it to feel the clock of the story.

rules.message: Type the character's name in capitals.
rules.why: A cue is always in capitals. The page shows it that way, but the file keeps what you typed, and the cast list and the breakdown match speakers by name — RAVI and Ravi should be one person, not two.

rules.message: This action runs past four lines — try breaking it up.
rules.why: Readers skim long blocks of description. Three or four lines at most, then a new paragraph, keeps the page moving and lets each paragraph read like one shot.

rules.message: Keep a parenthetical to one short line.
rules.why: A parenthetical is a small note on how a line is said — (quietly), (to Meena). Anything longer is action, and belongs in an action line above the cue.

rules.message: Start a parenthetical in lower case.
rules.why: By convention a parenthetical is lower case — (beat), (into the phone) — unless it begins with a name. It is a whisper in the margin, not a sentence.

rules.message: Wrap the parenthetical in brackets: (like this).
rules.why: The brackets are what make it read as a direction rather than part of the speech. The export adds any that are missing; adding them here keeps the page you see and the page you print the same.

rules.message: Who says this? Dialogue needs a character cue above it.
rules.why: Every speech sits under the name of the person speaking. Without a cue the actor cannot find their lines and the reader cannot tell who is talking. Add a Character element just above.
Transitions are written in capitals, like CUT TO:. The page shows it that way, but the file keeps what you typed.

rules.message: A transition ends in “TO:” — CUT TO:, DISSOLVE TO:.
rules.why: A transition says how we leave one scene for the next, and it ends with TO: and a colon. FADE IN:, FADE OUT. and CUT TO BLACK. are the usual exceptions. If this line describes something we see, it is action.

rules.message: Same speaker after action — add (CONT'D) to the cue.
rules.why: When a character keeps talking after a line of action, the cue gets (CONT'D) so the actor knows it is still one speech: RAVI (CONT'D).

rules.message: This scene runs past four pages.
rules.why: A page is about a minute on screen. A scene longer than four minutes is not wrong, but it is worth asking whether it is one scene or two, and whether every page earns its place.

ghosts.action: What we see, in the present tense.
ghosts.dialogue: What they say, the way they would say it.

levels.label: Coach
levels.hint: Hints, quiet format notes as you write, and the first-scene tour.

tour.title: Write your first scene
tour.intro: Six short steps, one for each kind of line in a screenplay. You write every word; the guide only says what goes where.
tour.done: That is a scene. Heading, action, a speaker, how they say it, what they say, and the way out — everything else in a screenplay is more of the same six. Keep going.

steps.title: 1 · Scene heading
steps.ask: Where are we, and when? Type INT. or EXT., the place, a dash, and DAY or NIGHT. Press Return when it is done.

steps.title: 2 · Action
steps.ask: What do we see? Describe it in the present tense, the way a camera would find it. Press Return when it is done.

steps.title: 3 · Character
steps.ask: Who speaks first? Make this line a Character and type their name in capitals.

steps.title: 4 · Parenthetical
steps.ask: How do they say it? A word or two in brackets — (quietly). Return after the name gives you dialogue, so switch it first.

steps.title: 5 · Dialogue
steps.ask: What do they say? Write it the way they would say it — Tanglish is welcome here.

steps.title: 6 · Transition
steps.ask: How do we leave? Make the next line a Transition and type CUT TO:.

panel.title: Format check
panel.clean: Nothing to flag. Every line reads the way a screenplay reads.
panel.empty: There is nothing to check yet.
